A source client can yield results and then cancel its stream before ownership transfers to the merge stage. The native execution node returns from its cancellation catch without disposing those results or returning its temporary reference buffer.

This PR applies the existing failure cleanup to the cancellation catch: dispose owned results, clear buffered references and return the buffer. Cancellation status and error suppression stay unchanged.

The response formatters write every JSON token straight into Kestrel's response `PipeWriter`, which takes a lock on each `GetSpan` and `Advance`, so a response pays thousands of lock operations.

Every formatter now writes through a `ChunkedPipeBufferWriter`: a 64 KB buffer that is copied to the pipe when it is full or the formatter flushes. The buffer is rented on the first write and returned as soon as it is copied, before the flush is awaited, so a stream holds nothing between events. A write of 4 KB or more goes to the pipe directly. The writer is cached per thread, so a response allocates nothing it did not allocate before. Flush points are unchanged: single results flush once at the end, streams per event.

Every result path borrows an `int[]` from the process-wide `PathSegmentPool`, and every rent and return takes its `SpinLock`. A request with nested lookups needs hundreds to thousands of paths, so with a few busy cores the threads spin on that lock, and `OperationPlanContext.Clean` returns every array through it once more.

The shared pool now rents and returns arrays in batches of 32, and the request-local pool stays alive in the pooled `FetchResultStore`: after a request it marks its arrays free again and returns only what exceeds `PathSegmentLocalPoolCapacity` (64 by default, 1 the minimum). A request touches the shared lock a few times instead of twice per path. The local pool shrinks its bookkeeping after a burst and drops its arrays when the shared pool has been replaced; the shared pool rejects arrays of another length without unbalancing its in-use count. A result document is detached from the local pool when the store hands its memory to the operation result, so a path read after execution is allocated and never touches another request's arrays. The local pool drops returns once every owned array is free, so a straggling return after a reset cannot hand the same array to two paths, and the shared pool holds its lock for at most 32 arrays per rent or return.

### Benchmarks

Each thread is one pooled request context with its own local pool, running requests back to back. A request rents the given number of paths, returns half and ends. Mean is the time per request on one thread.

## Summary

- A variable that the request does not send now counts as not provided wherever it is used as an input value, as the spec's input coercion and `CoerceArgumentValues` require. An input object field set to such a variable is left out of the coerced value, so the field's default applies or the field is absent. An argument set to one is treated like an omitted argument.
- `Optional<T>` therefore reports `HasValue = false` for these fields and arguments, and middleware that reads the argument literal no longer sees a `null` the client never sent.

## Behavioral changes

For a field or argument set to a variable that the request does not send:

| Area | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Optional<T>` field or argument, including mutation convention parameters | `HasValue = true`, value `null` or the default | `HasValue = false`, value `null` or the default |
| Argument literal (`ArgumentLiteral`, `ArgumentKind`) | Field present with `null` or the field default | Field absent |
| Filtering on a non-null field (`where: { name: { eq: $name } }`) | Error HC0026 | No condition |
| Filtering on a nullable field | Matches rows where the field is `null` | No condition |
| Sorting (`order: { name: $direction }`) | Error HC0026 | No ordering |

Unchanged:

- Values passed to resolver parameters and input properties that are not `Optional<T>`: `null` or the default, as before.
- A variable sent as `null`, and a variable with a default (including `= null`), still count as provided.
- An unsent variable used as a list item (`[$a, $b]`) still becomes `null`.
- Subgraphs behind Fusion behave the same way, since the gateway forwards an unsent variable as unsent.
- No public API changes.

Filtering on a nullable field is the only case where a query that succeeds today returns different results.

A 16.6.x backport also needs #10532, which is on `main` but not on `main-version-16-6`. Without it, an omitted filter variable produces an empty filter object, which fails with an unexpected error. #10424, which keeps a `= null` variable default distinct from an unsent variable, is already in 16.6.7.

## Test plan

- New spec tests cover an omitted variable in an input object field (alone, among other fields, and nested), in an argument, and with field and argument defaults. They also cover variables that have a value (`null`, a `= null` default, a `= "abc"` default), which must still count as set.
- New tests cover mutation conventions, in-memory filtering, and in-memory sorting with an omitted variable.
- Each new test fails without the fix. Disabling the field removal fails exactly the input field cases, and disabling the argument change fails exactly the argument cases.
- The Core execution, types, mutations, analyzer integration, cost analysis, ASP.NET Core, Data filtering, sorting, projections, EF Core, PostgreSQL, MongoDB filtering and sorting, and Fusion test suites pass on net10.0. The in-memory filtering suite, which has the new snapshot, passes on net8.0, net9.0, net10.0, and net11.0.

Closes #10530

When a request handler fails, Mocha answers the caller with a `NotAcknowledgedEvent` of kind `MessageKind.Fault`. With the Postgres outbox, the outbox processor only routed `MessageKind.Reply` through the transport's reply dispatch endpoint. A fault took the generic dispatch lookup instead, which cannot resolve a caller's reply queue, so the processor deleted the row and logged "Could not deserialize message body". `ScalarType.InputValueToLiteral` is supposed to store the `Utf8MemoryBuilder` that `JsonValueParser` creates on the context so that all values of a request share it. It checked a local that the parser never assigns, so the builder was never stored. Every numeric variable value created its own builder and rented a 1 KB array from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` that was never returned, because the coercion helper only seals a builder it finds on the context.

This PR stores the builder the parser created on the context, so later values reuse it and the helper seals it once per request, returning the pooled array. On a failed parse the parser keeps a builder it was given (`doNotSeal`), so the helper can still seal it, and abandons a builder it created itself, so that array goes back to the pool as well. An `Int` variable drops from 1,208 B to 192 B.

When the gateway resolves an entity lookup, `FetchResultStore` builds one set of variables per parent entity. Variable coercion allocated several objects for every field of an input object variable: `JsonVariableCoercion` read `JsonProperty.Name` up to three times per field (field lookup, error path segment and the coerced `ObjectFieldNode`), and each read decodes a new UTF-16 string. Every coerced field also got a new `NameNode`.

This PR looks input fields up by their raw UTF-8 property name. `FusionFieldDefinitionCollection<T>` gets a `TryGetField(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` overload: collections with up to eight accessible fields are scanned with `Ascii.Equals`, larger ones widen the name into a stack buffer and use the `ReadOnlySpan<char>` alternate lookup of the existing frozen dictionary. `FusionEnumValueCollection` does the same and drops its sorted byte index, so no collection keeps a second copy of its names. The coerced `ObjectFieldNode` reuses a `NameNode` cached on `FusionInputFieldDefinition`, and the error path uses the schema's field name. JSON allows escaping any character of a property name (`{"\u0069d": 1}` is a valid way to send `id`), so a property name containing an escape sequence falls back to the unescaped lookup, only when the UTF-8 lookup misses.

`JsonMarshal.GetRawUtf8PropertyName` exists since .NET 10, so net8.0 and net9.0 keep the string lookup. Per schema this adds the cached `NameNode` (40 B per input field definition) and one lookup struct per collection (16 B on net9.0 and later), nothing else.

When a receive endpoint stopped, in-flight handlers were never cancelled because `ReceiveContext` discarded the transport's cancellation token, so they kept running after shutdown began. Stopping also left PostgreSQL messages behind. A handler that finished after the stop began could not delete its message, because the delete used the already cancelled token, and messages that were leased but not finished stayed locked until the 5 minute lease timeout. Both were then redelivered and processed a second time. Finally, a transport or endpoint that failed to stop kept the remaining ones from stopping.

This PR passes the endpoint's cancellation token to handlers, including batch handlers, and keeps shutdown cancellation from triggering retries, fault handling or error logs. RabbitMQ and Azure Service Bus settle messages with `CancellationToken.None`, so an interrupted message is still nacked or abandoned. Batches are collected and processed per receive endpoint, so stopping one endpoint only cancels its own batches, and `MaxConcurrentBatches` now applies per endpoint.

The PostgreSQL endpoint deletes or releases a handled message with `CancellationToken.None`. A delete that fails after the handler completed is logged and the message is released with the error recorded. When polling is cancelled, the endpoint releases the messages of the current batch that it still holds and undoes their delivery count bump, so they are redelivered right away instead of after the lease timeout, and the interrupted attempt does not count toward max delivery.

`MessagingRuntime.StopAsync` and `MessagingTransport.StopAsync` keep stopping the remaining transports and endpoints when one fails, then rethrow the first failure. A transport that failed to stop stays started, so disposing the runtime tries it again. Disposal runs every remaining step when one fails and rethrows the first failure once everything is released, except a stop failure that an earlier stop already reported.
title: [Mocha] Cancel message handlers and release interrupted messages on shutdown

## Summary

Under `BindExplicitly()`, a send addressed by URI, `bus.SendAsync(message, new SendOptions { Endpoint = new Uri("rabbitmq:q/<name>") })`, failed with `InvalidOperationException("Queue not found")` unless `<name>` was declared in the sending host's own topology. The routing strategy created a dispatch endpoint configuration from the address, but `RabbitMQDispatchEndpoint.OnComplete` required the queue to be a topology resource, and in explicit mode the address-created endpoint does not add one. The only workaround was to declare every foreign queue locally with `DeclareQueue(name).AutoProvision(false)`.

A point-to-point send to a queue another service owns has no topology-ownership implication: the sender never declares, binds, or consumes the queue. 

## Change

- `RabbitMQDispatchEndpoint` resolves its target by name. A queue or exchange that is part of the topology is provisioned according to its auto-provision setting, as before. Any other target is published to by name, to the default exchange with the queue name as routing key or to the named exchange, and is never declared, bound, or consumed. The endpoint exposes `QueueName` and `ExchangeName`; `Queue`, `Exchange`, and `Destination` stay unset for a target outside the topology.
- `RabbitMQMessagingTransport.TryGetDispatchEndpoint` matches candidates by queue or exchange name instead of requiring `Destination is RabbitMQQueue`, so `rabbitmq://host/vhost/q/name` and `queue:name` resolve to the endpoint created from `rabbitmq:q/name`.
- The topology address parser moved from `RabbitMQRoutingStrategy` to `UriHelpers` so both call sites share it.
- `DiscoverTopology` and the explicit-mode guard are untouched. Nothing is added to the topology for an address-created endpoint.

### Behavior change

The dispatch endpoint is no longer gated by the topology at all. A configured `DispatchEndpoint("ep").ToQueue("name")` under explicit binding no longer fails at startup when the queue is not declared; it publishes by name. As with every RabbitMQ publish, a message the broker cannot route is dropped. A `mandatory`/`basic.return` hardening and a passive existence check were evaluated and deliberately left out; neither Wolverine nor the rest of Mocha verifies destinations at send time.

## Tests

- `RabbitMQDispatchEndpointTests`: address-created endpoints for undeclared queues and exchanges, the topology staying empty, alias resolution across address forms, and a declared `AutoProvision(false)` queue still binding to its topology resource.
- `RabbitMQDispatchProvisioningTests`: the publish goes to exchange `""` with the queue name as routing key, and no declare is issued.
- `Behaviors/ExternalDestinationTests` (real broker): a queue pre-created by another connection receives the send from a host that binds explicitly and declares nothing, and a send to a missing queue does not create it.

## Docs

- `routing-and-endpoints.md`: documents sends to queues outside the topology and fixes the address example, which used `rabbitmq://custom-inventory-queue`, a form no address parser accepts.
- `transports/rabbitmq.md`: the page claimed dispatch uses publisher confirms. The transport never enabled them, so the paragraph now states the actual behavior.

## Notes

- The second commit fixes pre-existing IDE1006/IDE0059 errors in Mocha example projects that are not part of `All.slnx`. Drop it if you prefer a strictly focused PR.
- The Azure Service Bus transport has the same gate for address-based sends under explicit binding; follow-up.
title: [Mocha] Fix RabbitMQ sends to undeclared queues failing under explicit binding

When the host shut down, `MessagingRuntimeHostedService.StopAsync` only disposed the consumers. The transports kept receiving and heartbeating, even after the service provider was disposed. Messages picked up after shutdown failed on the disposed consumers.

This PR adds `MessagingRuntime.StopAsync`, which stops the started transports, and the hosted service calls it instead of disposing the runtime. Disposing the runtime now stops and disposes its transports. A stopped runtime cannot be started again, so `StartAsync` throws after `StopAsync`. The PostgreSQL transport stops its background tasks in a new `OnAfterStopAsync` hook, so its consumer stays registered until the endpoints have stopped.
title: [Mocha] Fix transports not stopping when the host shuts down

body:
When the outbox opens a database connection to store a message, it leaves that connection open. An application may use a scoped context for the outbox and separate contexts from `IDbContextFactory` for repository operations, all within one `TransactionScope`. A later repository operation then opens another connection while the outbox connection is still open and can fail with “prepared transactions are disabled”.

The outbox now closes connections it opens after persistence, including on failure or cancellation. Connections already open remain open, and application writes and outbox messages still commit or roll back together.
title: [Mocha] Fix PostgreSQL outbox persistence connection lifetime

body:
When EF Core uses an `NpgsqlDataSource`, the PostgreSQL outbox and scheduling workers rebuild their data source from a connection string that omits the password by default (`Persist Security Info=false`). This loses credentials and authentication callbacks, causing authentication failures and leaving committed and scheduled messages undelivered. Both workers also keep a connection open while idle.

This PR clones the context's configured connection and reuses it while draining due messages, preserving authentication and data source settings. The connection and scope are disposed before idle waits, leaving the configured data source intact.
title: [Mocha] Fix PostgreSQL outbox and scheduling authentication with NpgsqlDataSource

## Summary

- Every response to a GET, HEAD, POST, or QUERY request on a GraphQL endpoint, other than a WebSocket upgrade, now lists `Accept` in `Vary`, whatever its status code and under every transport version. This covers `MapGraphQL`, `MapGraphQLHttp`, `MapGraphQLPersistedOperations`, and the Azure Functions pipeline. The endpoints select the response by `Accept` (the JSON media type, a single result as SSE or multipart when the client names it, and `406`) and copy `@cacheControl`'s `Cache-Control` onto it, so without `Vary` a shared or browser cache could hand one client's format to another.

The isolated-process Azure Functions adapter now replaces a response header that is set again, where it used to add a second copy of a multi-valued header and throw for a single-valued one such as `Content-Length`.
- The 16.6 to 16.7 migration guide lists the change under behavioral breaking changes, including that some CDNs (Akamai by default) do not cache responses whose `Vary` lists anything other than `Accept-Encoding`, with the workarounds. The transport and cache-control pages describe the header and how a custom formatter adds to it. No public API changes.

body:
We noticed in our telemetry that every now and then we log an unobserved exception. This happens particularly in subgraphs that operate under high load.

The exception is:
```
System.AggregateException: A Task's exception(s) were not observed either by Waiting on the Task or accessing its Exception property. As a result, the unobserved exception was rethrown by the finalizer thread. (Operations that change non-concurrent collections must have exclusive access. A concurrent update was performed on this collection and corrupted its state. The collection's state is no longer correct.)
 ---> System.InvalidOperationException: Operations that change non-concurrent collections must have exclusive access. A concurrent update was performed on this collection and corrupted its state. The collection's state is no longer correct.
   at System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary`2.FindValue(TKey key)
   at HotChocolate.Execution.Processing.WorkScheduler.Complete(IExecutionTask task)
   at HotChocolate.Execution.Processing.Tasks.ResolverTask.ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at HotChocolate.Execution.Processing.Tasks.ResolverTask.ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   --- End of inner exception stack trace ---
```

We traced the problem to the WorkScheduler and think that it happens as follows:
The `WorkScheduler.Complete` decrements the last resolver’s running count before acquiring `_sync` to update `_completed` and `_activePaths`. Meanwhile, `TryDispatchOrCompleteUnsafe` can acquire `_sync`, see no running work, and finish the request. Request cleanup can then clear those dictionaries while the resolver was still updating them.

The first commit adds a regression test for this ordering (this needed a hook into the WorkScheduler so feel free to reject that); the second moves the count decrement and bookkeeping into the same critical section.

Feel free to pick and choose whatever you want from this PR or throw it away and just treat it as an exploration 🙂
title: Fix a race condition in WorkScheduler

## Summary

- Every `text/event-stream` response ended with `event: complete` and no `data:` field. The browser `EventSource` API does not dispatch an event without data, so an `EventSource` client never saw `complete`: when the response ended it reconnected after its retry delay (3 s in Chromium) and the server executed the operation again, for as long as the page stayed open.
- The `complete` event now carries an empty `data:` field, as the [GraphQL over SSE RFC](https://github.com/graphql/graphql-over-http/blob/main/rfcs/GraphQLOverSSE.md) asks and the graphql-sse reference server writes. Clients that parse the stream themselves, including the 15.1 and 16.x readers in `GraphQLHttpClient` and the Fusion subgraph client, accept both forms, so a gateway and subgraph on different versions are unaffected.
- The 15 to 16 migration guide records the change as landing in 16.6.8, and the SSE docs describe the empty `data:` field.

## Test plan

- The pinned SSE bodies in `DeferOverHttpTests`, `GraphQLOverHttpSpecTests`, and `DeferredResultFormatterTests` expect the new line; they fail without the formatter change and pass with it.
- `ReadAsResultStream_Text_Event_Stream_Complete_With_Empty_Data_Ends_Stream` checks that `GraphQLHttpClient` stops reading at the new `complete` event.
- `HotChocolate.AspNetCore.Tests`, `HotChocolate.Transport.Http.Tests`, and `HotChocolate.Fusion.AspNetCore.Tests` pass on net10.0.
- In headless Chromium, an `EventSource` against Hot Chocolate re-ran `{ hello }` every 3 s; against the same bytes with the empty `data:` field it fired `complete` once and closed.
- graphql-sse 1.3.2 and 2.6.2 and `@urql/core` 6.0.3 return the same results for both forms.
title: Fix `EventSource` never receiving the SSE `complete` event

## Summary

- For a single result, `*/*` now covers only `application/graphql-response+json` and `application/json`. `multipart/mixed` and `text/event-stream` are selected only when the `Accept` header names them or their `multipart/*` or `text/*` range, because each frames the result in a protocol the client opts into: the incremental delivery framing, or GraphQL over SSE's `next` and `complete` events.
- A header that rejects both JSON types with `q=0` and names nothing else, such as `application/graphql-response+json;q=0, application/json;q=0, */*;q=1`, gets a bare `406` instead of a one-part `multipart/mixed`, or a one-event `text/event-stream` once multipart is rejected too. A header that rates the JSON types low but above `0` gets `application/graphql-response+json`. 16.6 answers both headers with `application/graphql-response+json`, so neither envelope answer has shipped in a stable release.
- The `406` is decided after execution, as it already is for `Accept: application/jsonl` on a query, because the pre-execution check grants every operation kind for `*/*`. Stream and subscription results are unaffected, and every header that names an envelope keeps its answer. The HTTP transport docs state the rule.

## Test plan

- New `GraphQLOverHttpSpecTests` rows pin the bare `406` for three wildcard-only headers and `application/graphql-response+json` for the low-quality JSON header under `Legacy`, `Draft20250508`, and `Draft20260903`. They failed before the change.
- Guard rows pin that naming an envelope still selects it. `multipart/mixed`, `multipart/*`, and `text/event-stream` at the default quality of `1` beat `application/json;q=0.5`, and each is selected beside `*/*` when both JSON types are rated `0`. A snapshot pins the single-result SSE body beside the existing multipart one. Widening the rule to skip `type/*` ranges, or applying it to stream results, fails these rows or existing `*/*` tests for deferred and subscription results.
- `HotChocolate.AspNetCore.Tests` passes on net8.0 through net11.0, and `HotChocolate.Fusion.AspNetCore.Tests` passes on net10.0.

## Summary

CI tests net11.0 only, so these failures show up only when the suite runs on every target framework.

- **Spatial tests on net8.0.** `PostgreSqlResource.RunSqlScriptAsync` opens its connection before the script runs, so Npgsql caches the database's types for that connection string without the ones the script creates (`geometry`, from `CREATE EXTENSION postgis`). EF Core 8 reuses that cache and fails with `The NpgsqlDbType 'Geometry' isn't present in your database`. `RunSqlScriptAsync` now calls `ReloadTypes()` after the script. The stale cache exists in every Npgsql version, so the reload runs on all target frameworks. It uses the synchronous overload because the resource compiles against Npgsql 8.0.7, while 9.0.x and 10.0.0 to 10.0.2 only have `ReloadTypesAsync(CancellationToken)`. Squadron ran scripts through `psql` inside the container, so this started with #10338.
- **`IsProjectedSelectorTests` on net8.0 and net9.0.** EF Core 8 and 9 translate the DataLoader key lookup to `IN (SELECT ... json_each(...))`, so the test now has that SQL as the inline snapshot for those target frameworks.
- **CookieCrumble `Match_StrictMode_Off` flake.** The test creates and deletes snapshot files whose names were shared by every target framework's test process, so one process could read a file another had just written. The global formatter registered by `SnapshotBuilder_Segment_Custom_Global_Serializer` made the contents differ when the two processes ran the tests in a different order. The file names now include the target framework.

## Test plan

- Both Spatial test projects, `IsProjectedSelectorTests`, and the CookieCrumble tests pass on net8.0, net9.0, net10.0, and net11.0.
- With plain Npgsql 8.0.7 and 10.0.0, a new connection opened after the script reads `geometry` as an unknown type, and as `public.geometry` after `ReloadTypes()`.
- The CookieCrumble failure reproduced every time by pre-creating another target framework's snapshot file before the fix. With per-framework file names, the test no longer reads it.

## Summary

- Variable coercion in Core and Fusion now applies an explicit `null` variable default (`$value: Int = null`) when the request omits the variable, as [Coercing Variable Values](https://spec.graphql.org/September2025/#sec-Coercing-Variable-Values) requires. Both helpers skipped a `null` default, so the variable was treated as not provided and an argument default such as `field(arg: Int = 5)` resolved to `5` instead of `null`. This regressed in #8931 and affects every release since 16.0.0.
- The Fusion gateway now sends the coerced `null` to the subgraph as an explicit variable value, so the result no longer depends on how the subgraph handles the forwarded `= null` default.
- Non-null variables are unaffected: validation already rejects a `null` default on them (`$a: Int! = null`).

## Test plan

- Core: a `VariableCoercionHelper` unit test for an omitted variable with a `null` default, and an `ArgumentCoercionTests` execution test where `echo(value: Int = 5)` returns `null`.
- Fusion: a `VariableCoercionHelper` unit test, and a gateway test whose snapshot shows the subgraph receiving `"value": null` and the response returning `null`.
- All four tests fail without the fix and pass with it on net10.0.
- The neighbouring coercion test classes (Core `VariableCoercionHelperTests`, `ArgumentCoercionTests`, `VariableCoercionIntegrationTests`, and `CodeFirstTests`; Fusion `VariableCoercionHelperTests` and `VariableCoercionTests`) pass, as do the existing tests that use `null` variable defaults (`IdAttributeTests` and `SlicingArgumentsTests`).

Closes #10423
title: Apply explicit null variable defaults when variables are omitted
